solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Joke about extremely unusual Russian prison system

indicators.note: about means the joke goes around the other letters

parts.note: a gag is a joke

indicators.note: extremely picks the extreme letters, first and last, of unusual

explanation.surface: A wry joke about the bizarre Soviet camp network.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gulag was the network of Soviet forced-labour camps, a prison system in Russia.

clue.text: Prickly bush: son's lost lots of blood

indicators.note: lost says the son has gone missing from the bush's letters

parts.note: gorse is a spiny yellow-flowered shrub
S is the abbreviation for son, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A son falls into a thorny bush and bleeds badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'son's lost' reads as 'son has lost': the S drops out of GORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Gore is shed blood, especially a large quantity from a wound.

clue.text: Wild animal spotted where golfers play, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word is taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: a links is a seaside golf course

explanation.surface: A wild cat is seen on the golf course, as rumour has it.
explanation.definitionFit: The lynx is a wild cat with a spotted coat, so the whole phrase describes it.

clue.text: Combination of hot dog and gin to make you sleep well

indicators.note: combination of says the letters of the two items are mixed together into a new order

explanation.surface: A late-night snack and a nightcap to send you off to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying goodnight is wishing someone to sleep well, the parting phrase at bedtime.

clue.text: Ring motoring organisation about group sharing vehicles

indicators.note: about says the ring and the club are turned round, read backwards

parts.note: a loop is a ring
the RAC is the Royal Automobile Club, a British motoring organisation

explanation.surface: Phoning a breakdown service about a car-sharing scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns LOOPRAC round; the RAC is Britain's Royal Automobile Club.
explanation.definitionFit: A car pool is an arrangement in which a group of people share their cars for journeys.

clue.text: Fraudster and match official coming up to talk together

parts.note: a con is a swindler, short for con man

indicators.note: coming up, in a down clue, says the official is read from bottom to top

parts.note: ref is short for referee

explanation.surface: A cheat and a referee approach to discuss a fix.
explanation.definitionFit: To confer is to discuss or consult with others, a synonym of the phrase.

clue.text: Dispute how to make progress in a boat

definitions.text: how to make progress in a boat

explanation.surface: An argument over how to get a boat moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Row rhymes with cow as a quarrel and with low as pulling oars; the two senses differ in sound.

clue.text: Surprised old woman married

parts.note: Vera is a woman's name
wed means married

explanation.surface: An elderly lady astonished to find herself a bride.
explanation.definitionFit: Overawed means struck with awe, so taken aback or amazed, close to surprised.

clue.text: Boy standing around there, covered in soap

indicators.note: standing around says the boy is placed around the other word

parts.note: a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A lad stands about in the bathroom, soaped all over.
explanation.definitionFit: To be lathered is to be coated in the foam that soap makes.

clue.text: Old Asian city controlled by fool

parts.note: ran, as in ran a business, means controlled
a goon is a fool

explanation.surface: A historic Asian capital governed by an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Rangoon is the former name of Yangon, the old capital of Myanmar (Burma).

clue.text: Cereal we hate mostly, when cooked

indicators.note: cooked suggests letters messed about and rearranged
mostly says most of the word is kept, its last letter dropped

explanation.surface: A grumble about breakfast food that is disliked once prepared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts HATE to HAT; 'when cooked' rearranges WE plus HAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheat is a cereal crop, the grain used for flour and bread.

clue.text: Highway in Tennesse's borders, say, following river

indicators.note: following puts the state after the river
borders takes only the outermost letters of the US state name

parts.note: R is the map abbreviation for river
Tennessee is an example of a state; say marks the example

explanation.surface: A road trip into Tennessee, along a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue misspells Tennessee; 'say' marks the next piece as an example, Tennessee being one state of many.
explanation.definitionFit: An interstate is a US highway running between states.

clue.text: Short Australian fellow, keen on the rules

indicators.note: short says the word loses its last letter

parts.note: Strine is the jokey name for Australian English
a gent is a fellow

explanation.surface: A small Aussie bloke who sticks to regulations.
explanation.walkthrough: Strine, a play on how an Australian says 'Australian', means Australian slang; 'Short' cuts it to STRIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Stringent means strict and exacting, so someone insistent that rules are followed.

clue.text: Band leader helps some orchestra members

indicators.note: leader takes the leading, first letter of the word band

parts.note: assists means helps

explanation.surface: A bandleader lends a hand to orchestral players.
explanation.definitionFit: Bassists play the double bass, found in the string section of an orchestra.

clue.text: Be friends? You must be joking

definitions.meaning: to be on good terms with someone
a dismissive exclamation of disbelief, as in 'away with you!'

explanation.surface: Two responses to a proposed friendship, one warm and one scornful.
explanation.definitionFit: To get along is to be on good terms; 'get along with you!' is an old expression of disbelief.

clue.text: Get one's own back, coming out of Geneva

indicators.note: coming out of suggests the city's letters are knocked out of shape and rearranged

explanation.surface: Taking revenge after leaving the Swiss city.
explanation.definitionFit: To avenge is to take revenge, getting even for a wrong.

clue.text: French cheeses, might one say, for a picnic

indicators.note: might one say marks a sound-alike for the cheeses

parts.note: Brie is a soft French cheese; plural bries

explanation.surface: Packing French cheeses for an outdoor meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picnic' is not the meal but the idiom: 'no picnic' means hard, so 'a picnic' is something easy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal terms for a task that is very easy.

clue.text: Member of university staff gets it as financial benefit

parts.note: prof is short for professor

explanation.surface: A professor earns money from an outside venture.
explanation.definitionFit: Profit is money gained, a financial return over costs.

clue.text: Milliner comes in to celebrate? Smashing!

indicators.note: comes in says the milliner enters the middle of the other word

parts.note: to sing can mean to celebrate in song
a hatter makes hats, as a milliner does

explanation.surface: A hat-maker arrives at a party, which turns out to be great.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashing' looks like British praise but means breaking into pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Shattering means breaking violently into pieces, the same as smashing.

clue.text: Hardly an attractive place to take the plunge

explanation.surface: Plunging into a seedy joint, metaphorically or literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A dive is a squalid bar; to dive is to plunge headlong.

clue.text: Old mortgage deal, in part

indicators.note: in part says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An outdated home-loan agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: Aged means elderly, having lived long, a synonym of old.

clue.text: Writer from Swiss Cottage

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the place name

explanation.surface: An author hails from a district of north London.
explanation.walkthrough: Swiss Cottage is an area of north London.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter Scott was a Scottish novelist and poet, author of Ivanhoe.

clue.text: Striker regularly missing match

indicators.note: regularly missing drops every other letter of the footballer word, keeping the rest

explanation.surface: A footballer absent from the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'match' is not a game but a verb sense: to tie is to equal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie is a match between teams, as in a cup tie.

clue.text: Thinking Europeans should link during Scottish dance

indicators.note: during puts the Europeans within the dance

parts.note: the Highland fling is a Scottish dance
E stands for European, twice for the plural

explanation.surface: European visitors joining hands at a ceilidh.
explanation.definitionFit: A feeling is an opinion or belief, what one is thinking.

clue.text: Imply American rejected scrambled eggs and toast for starters

indicators.note: rejected says the word is sent back, reversed

parts.note: US means American

indicators.note: scrambled tells us the letters are jumbled
for starters takes the starting letter of toast

explanation.surface: An American turning down a breakfast of eggs on toast.
explanation.definitionFit: To suggest is to hint at or indicate indirectly, the same as imply.

clue.text: Put foot down: student finally to study

indicators.note: finally takes the final letter of student

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it at university

explanation.surface: A student getting firm about revising at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put foot down' suggests being firm, but here it is literal stepping.
explanation.definitionFit: To tread is to step, setting a foot down on the ground.
